text.body: From March 4, the library will close at 5 p.m. on Saturdays instead of 8 p.m. Sunday hours are unchanged (noon to 6 p.m.). Books may still be returned at any time using the drop box beside the main entrance. Study rooms must now be booked online at least one day in advance; walk-in bookings will no longer be accepted.

text.title: Urban Heat Islands
text.body:
Cities are often several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. The main cause is the replacement of vegetation with materials such as asphalt and concrete, which absorb sunlight during the day and release it slowly at night. Because of this, the temperature difference between a city and its surroundings is usually greatest after sunset rather than at midday.

Human activity adds to the effect. Cars, air conditioners and factories all release heat directly into the air. Tall buildings also play a role: they trap warm air between them and reduce wind speed at street level.

Cities are experimenting with several solutions. Painting roofs white reflects sunlight back into the atmosphere, and planting trees provides shade while cooling the air through evaporation. Some researchers argue that such measures could reduce peak summer temperatures by up to two degrees, which would lower both energy use and heat-related illness.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, when is the temperature difference between a city and the countryside usually largest?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: the difference 'is usually greatest after sunset rather than at midday'.

questions.prompt: The word "release" in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to
questions.explanation: Materials absorb heat and then 'release' (give off) it at night.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention tall buildings?
options: To show that cities use too much energy
To argue that cities should be smaller
To explain another way cities stay warm
To describe how wind is produced
questions.explanation: Buildings are another cause: they trap warm air and reduce wind.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a solution?
questions.explanation: White roofs (reflective surfaces) and trees are mentioned; lowering buildings is not.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about the proposed solutions?
options: They have already removed the heat island effect.
They increase energy use in summer.
They work only in small towns.
questions.explanation: Lower temperatures would reduce 'heat-related illness', a health benefit.

text.title: The Origins of Writing
text.body:
Writing appears to have developed independently in at least three places: Mesopotamia, China and Mesoamerica. In Mesopotamia, the earliest written records were not literature but accounts. Clay tokens representing goods such as grain or sheep were used to track trade, and over time these tokens were replaced by marks pressed into clay tablets.

Initially, each sign represented a whole object or idea. Such a system, however, requires thousands of signs and is difficult to learn. Scribes gradually began to use some signs for their sound rather than their meaning, so that a symbol could be combined with others to spell words that had no simple picture. This shift toward phonetic writing made it possible to record names, grammar and eventually stories.

The consequences were far-reaching. Laws could be fixed in a permanent form, knowledge could be passed across generations without relying on memory, and governments could administer larger territories. Yet for centuries literacy remained limited to a small group of trained specialists.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what was the original purpose of writing in Mesopotamia?
questions.explanation: The earliest records were 'accounts' of goods like grain and sheep.

questions.prompt: Why did scribes begin to use signs for their sounds?
options: Pictures could not represent every word easily.
questions.explanation: A system of whole-word signs needs thousands of signs; sound signs could spell words without a simple picture.

questions.prompt: The word "administer" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to
questions.explanation: To administer a territory is to manage or govern it.

questions.prompt: What does the final sentence suggest?
options: Most people could not read for a long time.
Literacy declined after laws were written.
questions.explanation: Literacy 'remained limited to a small group' for centuries.

tasks.context: Listen to a conversation between a student and a housing office employee.

audio.text: Hi, I'm having a problem with the heating in my dorm room. It's been cold for three days.

audio.speaker: Employee
audio.text: I'm sorry to hear that. Have you filled out a maintenance request online?

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: I did, on Monday, but nobody has come yet.

audio.speaker: Employee
audio.text: Let me check. Ah, I see it. It looks like it was sent to the wrong building. I'll mark it urgent and send it to the right team now.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: Thank you. Is there anything I can do in the meantime?

audio.speaker: Employee
audio.text: We have portable heaters you can borrow. Just bring your student ID to the front desk.

questions.prompt: Why was the student's problem not fixed?

The request went to the wrong building.
The repair team was on holiday.
The heater was too old to repair.
questions.explanation: The employee finds the request 'was sent to the wrong building'.

questions.explanation: She is told to bring her student ID to borrow a portable heater.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a talk in a biology class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Today I want to talk about how plants defend themselves. Since plants can't run away, they've developed other strategies. Some, like cacti, rely on physical defences such as spines. But many plants use chemistry instead. When a caterpillar starts eating a tomato leaf, for example, the plant produces chemicals that make the leaves harder to digest. What's really interesting is that the damaged plant also releases substances into the air. Nearby tomato plants detect these signals and begin preparing their own defences before they're even attacked. So, in a sense, plants are warning their neighbours.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.explanation: The professor opens with 'how plants defend themselves'.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention cacti?
options: To compare their chemistry with tomatoes
As an example of a physical defence
As an example of a plant without defences
questions.explanation: Cacti with spines illustrate physical defences.

questions.prompt: What happens when a tomato plant is damaged?
questions.explanation: The damaged plant 'releases substances into the air'.

questions.prompt: What does the professor imply when he says plants are "warning their neighbours"?
options: Nearby plants respond before being attacked.
questions.explanation: Neighbouring plants prepare defences 'before they're even attacked'.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a talk in an economics class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Let's look at something economists call the anchoring effect. When people estimate a value, they're heavily influenced by the first number they see, even if that number is irrelevant. In one well-known experiment, participants spun a wheel that landed on either ten or sixty-five, and were then asked to estimate a percentage. Those who saw sixty-five gave much higher estimates. Now, retailers use this all the time. A jacket labelled 'was three hundred dollars, now one fifty' feels like a bargain, even if the original price was never realistic. The lesson for consumers is to decide what something is worth to you before you look at the price tag.

questions.prompt: What is the anchoring effect?
options: Being influenced by the first number seen
Spending more when shopping with others
questions.explanation: People are 'heavily influenced by the first number they see'.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor describe the wheel experiment?
options: To show that games affect mood
To explain how percentages are calculated
To demonstrate that irrelevant numbers affect estimates
questions.explanation: The random wheel number changed participants' estimates.

questions.prompt: What does the professor imply about the jacket's original price?
options: It may have been set artificially high.
It was a mistake by the store.
It was lower than the sale price.
It was the average market price.
questions.explanation: 'Even if the original price was never realistic' implies it was inflated to act as an anchor.

questions.prompt: What advice does the professor give?
options: Decide an item's value before seeing the price
questions.explanation: 'Decide what something is worth to you before you look at the price tag.'

students.post: I think recordings are very helpful. When I miss something during a lecture, I can go back and listen again. This is especially useful for students whose first language is not English.
